power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .096", Sentence = "However, no significant differences were found between the original six-item composite and the measurement-aligned composite of the same two dimensions (BH-adjusted p = .096-.937; Table S30)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

Thank you Thank you for your interest in participating in this study. This study is run by an international team of researchers and is led by researchers at Harvard University and the University of Zurich. Before you begin, it is important that you are informed about the purpose and procedure of this research. Please read the following information carefully. Purpose of this research The purpose of this research is to gain insights into people’s attitudes and their opinions about science. This research can help us to better understand how people view science. What to expect from this study You will be asked to answer questions on your attitudes and opinions about science. We will also ask you an open-ended question that will give you the possibility to elaborate on your answers. Lastly, you will also be asked to answer questions on climate change. Guidance on how to answer questions will be provided. Anonymity No personally identifying information will be collected. Any research data published in scientific journals or elsewhere will be anonymous and cannot be traced back to you. This completely anonymized data will be made publicly available. About this study Participation will take about 15 minutes. You participate voluntarily and can choose not to take part. You can agree to take part and later change your mind. Your decision will not be held against you. You can ask all the questions you want before you decide. If you have questions, concerns, or complaints, please contact: Dr. Viktoria Cologna Harvard University tisp.manylabs@gmail.com By selecting "I consent to participate", you consent to the terms and conditions described above.

Before you begin, it is important that you are informed about the purpose and procedure of this research. Please read the following information carefully. Purpose of this research The purpose of this research is to gain insights into people’s attitudes and their opinions about science. This research can help us to better understand how people view science. What to expect from this study You will be asked to answer questions on your attitudes and opinions about science. We will also ask you an open-ended question that will give you the possibility to elaborate on your answers. Lastly, you will also be asked to answer questions on climate change. Guidance on how to answer questions will be provided. Anonymity No personally identifying information will be collected. Any research data published in scientific journals or elsewhere will be anonymous and cannot be traced back to you. This completely anonymized data will be made publicly available. About this study Participation will take about 15 minutes. You participate voluntarily and can choose not to take part. You can agree to take part and later change your mind. Your decision will not be held against you. You can ask all the questions you want before you decide. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).
#### Reproducible Environment
The repository pins its analysis environment via a `sessionInfo()` record. Declared R version: 4.3.1.
#### Parsable code
All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

data_check.summary_text:
-  We classified 184 files: 40 data, 40 code, 6 documentation, 98 materials.
-  We found 40 tabular data files and extracted 862 columns from 13 of them.
-  We grouped the files into 2 study groups (ex1, ex2), plus 2 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).
-  8 tabular data files could not be read because they were not downloaded. This can happen for private repositories or failed downloads; you can also pass `local_path` to point at a local copy.
-  Repository https://osf.io/5c3qd exceeds the 500 MB per-repository budget: downloaded the smallest files up to the cap, 2 files omitted. Raise `max_download_size` to include more.
-  1 file read as a table but is not a usable rectangular dataset (ds_id.sav: 100% of columns are free text, not variables). No columns were extracted and they were not sent to the LLM. Share the underlying data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable) with a codebook: ds_id.sav. We ran automated data-quality checks on 862 columns; 171 columns have at least one potential issue (154 columns with numeric values stored as text; 14 columns with leading/trailing whitespace; 12 columns with inconsistent category casing; 12 columns of free text that may contain personal detail; 12 columns whose values look like personal information; 4 columns with values in a legacy (non-UTF-8) encoding; 3 columns with no observed values (entirely empty)). We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender. 2 of 2 spreadsheet files have at least one formatting issue (colour coding, merged cells, empty rows/columns, or an offset header).

#### Data Files

#### Descriptives Overview

We found 717 columns with at least one missing value. 3 columns are empty (no values in any row); store data without empty columns.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 862 columns across 14 data files.
#### Issues Identified

175 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Spreadsheet Formatting
We examined 2 spreadsheet files in the repository; 2 have at least one formatting issue.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("ds_popdata_edu.xls", "ds_popdata_sex.xlsx", 
"ds_popdata_sex.xlsx", "ds_popdata_sex.xlsx", "ds_popdata_sex.xlsx", 
"ds_popdata_sex.xlsx"), Sheet = c(NA, "Estimates", "Estimates", 
"Medium variant", "Medium variant", "NOTES"), Issue = c("Un-inspectable (.xls)", 
"Empty rows", "Empty or unnamed columns", "Empty rows", "Empty or unnamed columns", 
"Colour coding"), Detail = c("Legacy .xls format: colour, merged cells and empty rows/columns cannot be inspected. Convert to .xlsx or .ods for a full check.", 
"2 fully empty rows inside the data range.", "64 columns are empty or have a blank header.", 
"2 fully empty rows inside the data range.", "64 columns are empty or have a blank header.", 
"1 cell uses fill colour to encode information; colour is lost on CSV export."
)), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE)
```

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 14 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Shkenca dhe përfitimet e saj.



Unë mendoj se njerëzimi përfiton shumë nga shkenca për shkak të natyrës së saj të ndryshme nga fushat e tjera të njohurive dhe praktikave njerëzore. Shkenca përdor metodat e vëzhgimit dhe testimin e ideve në mënyrë sistematike dhe racionale, duke u bazuar në logjikën dhe provat shtojnë të vlefshme, e cila ndihmon në zbulimin dhe kuptimin e legjislacionit të natyrës dhe të botës në përgjithësi.

Kjo dije dhe kuptim i sjellë nga shkenca mund të përdoret për të zgjidhur problemet komplekse dhe për të krijuar teknologji të reja dhe inovacione që mund të ndryshojnë jetën tonë në mënyra pozitive. Për shembull, shkenca ka mundësuar zhvillimin e teknologjisë informative dhe komunikative, mjekësisë moderne, teknologjisë së energjisë së rinovueshme dhe shumë fushave të tjera që kanë ndikuar thellësisht në jetën dhe mirëqenien tonë.

Përfitimet e shkencës shkojnë edhe më tutje, duke ndihmuar në zhvillimin e dijeve dhe teknologjive që mund të ndikojnë në të ardhmen tonë. Shkenca gjithashtu mund të na ndihmojë të kuptojmë sfidat e jetës dhe të planetit tonë dhe të ndërmarrim veprime për të zgjidhur këto sfida në mënyra që janë të qëndrueshme dhe të përshtatshme për planetin tonë.

Pra, mund të themi se njerëzimi përfiton shumë nga shkenca dhe vazhdon të përfitojë, sepse na ndihmon të zgjidhim probleme të mëdha dhe të krijojmë një botë më të mirë dhe më të qëndrueshme për të gjithë ne dhe planetin tonë.", "Njerezit

Shkenca dhe përfitimet e saj.



Unë mendoj se njerëzimi përfiton shumë nga shkenca për shkak të natyrës së saj të ndryshme nga fushat e tjera të njohurive dhe praktikave njerëzore. Shkenca përdor metodat e vëzhgimit dhe testimin e ideve në mënyrë sistematike dhe racionale, duke u bazuar në logjikën dhe provat shtojnë të vlefshme, e cila ndihmon në zbulimin dhe kuptimin e legjislacionit të natyrës dhe të botës në përgjithësi.

Kjo dije dhe kuptim i sjellë nga shkenca mund të përdoret për të zgjidhur problemet komplekse dhe për të krijuar teknologji të reja dhe inovacione që mund të ndryshojnë jetën tonë në mënyra pozitive. Për shembull, shkenca ka mundësuar zhvillimin e teknologjisë informative dhe komunikative, mjekësisë moderne, teknologjisë së energjisë së rinovueshme dhe shumë fushave të tjera që kanë ndikuar thellësisht në jetën dhe mirëqenien tonë.

Përfitimet e shkencës shkojnë edhe më tutje, duke ndihmuar në zhvillimin e dijeve dhe teknologjive që mund të ndikojnë në të ardhmen tonë. Shkenca gjithashtu mund të na ndihmojë të kuptojmë sfidat e jetës dhe të planetit tonë dhe të ndërmarrim veprime për të zgjidhur këto sfida në mënyra që janë të qëndrueshme dhe të përshtatshme për planetin tonë.

Pra, mund të themi se njerëzimi përfiton shumë nga shkenca dhe vazhdon të përfitojë, sepse na ndihmon të zgjidhim probleme të mëdha dhe të krijojmë një botë më të mirë dhe më të qëndrueshme për të gjithë ne dhe planetin tonë.", "Njerezit

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **22 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). text.text: In a reanalysis of perceived scientist trustworthiness across 68 countries/regions, measurement-aligned indicated limitations in the cross-national comparability of the original measurement structure.

Some country/region rankings and predictor associations varied across alternative scoring approaches, suggesting the value of considering measurement invariance when interpreting cross-national findings.
Future research could use diverse methods to strengthen crosscultural measurement validity.
Large-scale cross-national and big-team science studies integrate data from diverse contexts, increasing the possibility that common measures function differently across countries and regions.
If such variation is not adequately considered, observed rankings and associations may partly reflect measurement non-invariance rather than substantive differences.
Given the policy and public relevance of such findings, greater attention to measurement invariance (MI) is warranted.
Whether MI is a necessary condition for meaningful cross-national comparison remains debated.
One view holds that concerns about non-invariance may be overstated and that valid comparisons can remain possible under some forms of imperfect equivalence (Welzel et al., 2023).
text.formatted: One view holds that concerns about non-invariance may be overstated and that valid comparisons can remain possible under some forms of imperfect equivalence <ref type="bibr">(Welzel et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A contrasting view emphasizes that non-invariance can affect latent means, rankings, associations, and nomological validity in ways that are difficult to distinguish from substantive group differences (Meuleman et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A contrasting view emphasizes that non-invariance can affect latent means, rankings, associations, and nomological validity in ways that are difficult to distinguish from substantive group differences <ref type="bibr">(Meuleman et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This debate has recently extended to cross-cultural psychology, with Kusano et al. (2025) questioning conventional invariance requirements and Sterner and Goretzko (2026) underscoring the consequences of non-invariance for comparability.

(2025)</ref> questioning conventional invariance requirements and <ref type="bibr">Sterner and Goretzko (2026)</ref> underscoring the consequences of non-invariance for comparability.

text.text: The present study examines the sensitivity of crossnational findings to how measurement non-invariance is handled through a reanalysis of Cologna et al. (2025), who assessed perceived scientist trustworthiness among 69,534 respondents in 68 countries/regions.
text.formatted: The present study examines the sensitivity of crossnational findings to how measurement non-invariance is handled through a reanalysis of <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Cologna et al. (2025)</ref>, who assessed perceived scientist trustworthiness among 69,534 respondents in 68 countries/regions.

text.text: We reanalyzed the original dataset in three steps (Supplementary Fig. S1 and Table S1).
text.formatted: We reanalyzed the original dataset in three steps (Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref> and Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: First, we evaluated MI for the 12-item measure of perceived scientist trustworthiness using two strategies: a pooled confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) including all countries/regions, followed by multigroup MI testing across the full sample; and country/region specific CFAs used as a screening step, after which only countries/regions with acceptable CFA fit were included in the subsequent multigroup MI testing.

Second, where scalar invariance was not supported, we applied measurement alignment (MA) to accommodate partial non-invariance and compared the resulting estimates with those reported in the original article based on weighted observed scores.
Third, all analyses were repeated with and without survey weights.
For the four-factor perceived scientist trustworthiness model, configural and metric invariance were supported, whereas scalar and strict invariance were not (Supplementary Table S4).
text.formatted: For the four-factor perceived scientist trustworthiness model, configural and metric invariance were supported, whereas scalar and strict invariance were not (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: A partialinvariance model did not converge.
We therefore implemented four MA specifications following Han (2024).
text.formatted: We therefore implemented four MA specifications following <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Han (2024)</ref>.

text.text: The main text reports the specification most closely corresponding to the original CFA model (Path B1, Step 5 in Fig. S1); the remaining results are provided in Supplementary Tables S5-S10.
text.formatted: The main text reports the specification most closely corresponding to the original CFA model <ref type="bibr">(Path B1,</ref> <ref type="bibr">Step 5</ref> in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>); the remaining results are provided in Supplementary Tables <ref type="table">S5-S10</ref>.

text.text: Admissible aligned solutions were obtained for benevolence and openness, which were retained for subsequent ranking and correlational analyses.

To assess the impact of factor reduction, we compared rankings and regression results across three scores based on the same sample: the original four-factor score, a six-item unaligned score from the two retained factors, and the aligned two-factor score (see
The results showed that alignment preserved the broad ordering while altering the specific rank positions of many countries.

The overall rank ordering was consistent (Spearman's ρ = .971; Kendall's τ = .863), but 62 of 68 countries/regions (91.2%) still changed their exact rank position after alignment, with a median absolute displacement of 3 positions (IQR = 1.75-5; range = 0-15).
The unaligned twofactor score and the aligned two-factor score showed greater overall similarity; however, 36 countries still changed their rank positions (Table 1; Supplementary Table S15).
text.formatted: The unaligned twofactor score and the aligned two-factor score showed greater overall similarity; however, 36 countries still changed their rank positions (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>; Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S15</ref>).

text.text: The significant negative association with science-related populist attitudes in the original article (Fig. 2, p. 716) was not replicated using aligned scores (Supplementary Table S25, Block 3).
text.formatted: The significant negative association with science-related populist attitudes in the original article (Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>, p. 716) was not replicated using aligned scores (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S25</ref>, Block 3).

text.text: Direct comparison based on the same sample confirmed a significant difference between the original and aligned scores (Δβ = -0.033, 95% CI [-0.040, -0.026], BH-adjusted p < .001; Supplementary Table S29).
text.formatted: Direct comparison based on the same sample confirmed a significant difference between the original and aligned scores (Δβ = -0.033, 95% CI [-0.040, -0.026], BH-adjusted p < .001; Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S29</ref>).

text.text: Pairwise comparisons revealed significant differences in regression coefficients between the original score and both the unaligned and aligned two-factor scores, but not between the two-factor scores themselves (Supplementary TableS30).
Moreover, some predictors, including science-related populist attitudes, were not tested for MI, which may also affect cross-national regression estimates (Yan & Ma, 2026).
text.formatted: Moreover, some predictors, including science-related populist attitudes, were not tested for MI, which may also affect cross-national regression estimates <ref type="bibr">(Yan & Ma, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these findings highlight two considerations for large-scale cross-national research.
First, uncertainty regarding measurement comparability warrants caution when interpreting country/region rankings and substantive associations.

In our study, measurement alignment did not yield an acceptable solution for all factors: two of the four original factors could not be successfully aligned, suggesting possible limitations in their cross-national comparability.
Our findings indicate that, in such situations, different analytical choices may lead to different results and interpretations.
In the present study, we reported country/region rankings and regression results under three different analytical strategies.
These findings may suggest that examining measurement invariance can help clarify the structure of the measure and provide a basis for a more cautious interpretation of subsequent analyses.
Second, the measurement framework used in the original article was developed using U.S.
online samples (Besley et al., 2026), raising questions about its conceptual equivalence across 68 culturally, politically, and institutionally diverse countries/regions.
text.formatted: online samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Besley et al., 2026)</ref>, raising questions about its conceptual equivalence across 68 culturally, politically, and institutionally diverse countries/regions.

text.text: Future cross-cultural measure development may integrate qualitative and mixed-method evidence to help clarify how the focal construct is understood across contexts and which cues inform respondents' judgments.

Such evidence may guide item refinement, factor-structure evaluation, and subsequent psychometric validation, thereby strengthening cross-cultural validity and the interpretation of cross-context comparisons.

In summary, the credibility of large-scale comparative findings depends not only on sample size, geographic coverage, and analytic sophistication, but also on the conceptual and psychometric comparability of the constructs examined.
Measurement comparability merits consideration when interpreting global comparative findings. Yan, X., & Ma, Z. (2026).

In group comparisons, researchers frequently presume that the instruments share an equivalent measurement structure.
The soundness of this presumption is essential for interpreting group-related difference (Vandenberg & Lance, 2000).
text.formatted: The soundness of this presumption is essential for interpreting group-related difference <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Vandenberg & Lance, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Without measurement invariance, one cannot confidently maintain that the construct has the same meaning across groups (Little, 1997).
text.formatted: Without measurement invariance, one cannot confidently maintain that the construct has the same meaning across groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Little, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, comparisons of means or structural parameters should be based on measurement models that function similarly across groups (Ployhart & Oswald, 2004).
text.formatted: Accordingly, comparisons of means or structural parameters should be based on measurement models that function similarly across groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Ployhart & Oswald, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: We noted that current studies differ in how they operationalize cross-group measurement invariance testing.

On the one hand, because configural invariance is typically regarded as the foundation for subsequent, higher levels of measurement invariance (Byrne, 2013; Putnick & Bornstein, 2016), some researchers diagnose the measurement model within each group before fitting a multi-group model, in order to identify and address potential problems that may lead to estimation failure or unacceptable solutions.
text.formatted: On the one hand, because configural invariance is typically regarded as the foundation for subsequent, higher levels of measurement invariance <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Byrne, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Putnick & Bornstein, 2016)</ref>, some researchers diagnose the measurement model within each group before fitting a multi-group model, in order to identify and address potential problems that may lead to estimation failure or unacceptable solutions.

text.text: In extreme cases, when certain groups show serious data-quality issues, or when the model is not identified / yields unacceptable solutions that cannot be resolved through reasonable modifications, researchers may exclude these groups from cross-group comparability inferences (Cosma et al., 2022; Sawicki et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In extreme cases, when certain groups show serious data-quality issues, or when the model is not identified / yields unacceptable solutions that cannot be resolved through reasonable modifications, researchers may exclude these groups from cross-group comparability inferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cosma et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Sawicki et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, others have argued that when a large number of groups are involved (e.g., cross-national or large-scale surveys), requiring every group to achieve a traditionally defined "good fit" is often unrealistic (Rutkowski & Svetina, 2014).
text.formatted: On the other hand, others have argued that when a large number of groups are involved (e.g., cross-national or large-scale surveys), requiring every group to achieve a traditionally defined "good fit" is often unrealistic <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Rutkowski & Svetina, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, some researchers do not screen groups via separate single-group CFAs prior to invariance testing; instead, they fit a multigroup CFA (MG-CFA) including all groups simultaneously, beginning with the configural (baseline) model and then imposing equality constraints to evaluate measurement invariance (Hirschfeld & Brachel, 2014).
text.formatted: Accordingly, some researchers do not screen groups via separate single-group CFAs prior to invariance testing; instead, they fit a multigroup CFA (MG-CFA) including all groups simultaneously, beginning with the configural (baseline) model and then imposing equality constraints to evaluate measurement invariance <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hirschfeld & Brachel, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Considering that Cologna et al. (2025) conducted CFA simultaneously across all countries when testing measurement invariance, we decided to adopt two different CFA strategies (see Fig. S1).
text.formatted: Considering that <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Cologna et al. (2025)</ref> conducted CFA simultaneously across all countries when testing measurement invariance, we decided to adopt two different CFA strategies (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: Specifically, we evaluated the four-factor model of perceived scientist trustworthiness using two CFA strategies: (a) a pooled, multi-country CFA in which all countries were analyzed simultaneously, and (b) separate CFAs conducted within each of the 68 countries/regions.

For the country-specific approach, the four-factor CFA was first fitted separately within each country, and only countries with acceptable model fit were retained for subsequent multigroup measurement invariance testing.

Following established recommendations (Bentler & Bonett, 1980; Brown, 2015; Hu & Bentler, 1999; Schermelleh-Engel et al., 2003), model fit was evaluated using multiple indices, including the comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR).
text.formatted: Following established recommendations <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bentler & Bonett, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Brown, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hu & Bentler, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Schermelleh-Engel et al., 2003)</ref>, model fit was evaluated using multiple indices, including the comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR).

text.text: Two sets of thresholds were applied: Criterion 1 (CFI ≥ 0.90, TLI ≥ 0.90, RMSEA ≤ 0.08, SRMR ≤ 0.10) and Criterion 2 (CFI ≥ 0.95, TLI ≥ 0.95, RMSEA ≤ 0.08, SRMR ≤ 0.10).

We noted that Cologna et al. (2025) provided and applied post-stratification weights in their data analysis strategy to align statistical estimates more closely with the target population distributions on key demographic variables such as sex, age, and education.
text.formatted: We noted that <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Cologna et al. (2025)</ref> provided and applied post-stratification weights in their data analysis strategy to align statistical estimates more closely with the target population distributions on key demographic variables such as sex, age, and education.

text.text: Poststratification/calibration weights are primarily used to reduce bias arising from sample selection and nonresponse by matching the sample to known marginal or joint distributions of auxiliary variables (e.g., sex, age, education), thereby improving the population representativeness of point estimates (e.g., means, regression coefficients).

However, obtaining appropriate variances and standard errors depends on using suitable design-based variance estimation methods and on assumptions such as approximate randomness within post-strata (Battaglia et al., 2009).
text.formatted: However, obtaining appropriate variances and standard errors depends on using suitable design-based variance estimation methods and on assumptions such as approximate randomness within post-strata <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Battaglia et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, incorporating weights in structural equation modeling and multi-group CFA can affect parameter estimates, standard errors, and fit statistics.

This concern is particularly salient when weights are primarily derived from post-stratification calibration rather than from a clearly specified probability sampling design, in which case the appropriateness of the weighting scheme and its impact on substantive conclusions should be evaluated via sensitivity analyses (Asparouhov, 2005).
text.formatted: This concern is particularly salient when weights are primarily derived from post-stratification calibration rather than from a clearly specified probability sampling design, in which case the appropriateness of the weighting scheme and its impact on substantive conclusions should be evaluated via sensitivity analyses <ref type="bibr">(Asparouhov, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, to assess the robustness of measurement-model fit and measurement-invariance conclusions to weighting decisions, we report results from both weighted and unweighted analyses in our primary models: the weighted analyses used the country-level ("WEIGHT_CNTRY") or the pooled-sample ("WEIGHT_GLOBL").

Under the country-specific CFA approach, when sampling weights were applied, 37 countries met Criterion 1 and 24 countries met Criterion 2; when sampling weights were not applied, 56 countries met Criterion 1 and 34 countries met Criterion 2 (see Fig. S1, Step 3).
text.formatted: Under the country-specific CFA approach, when sampling weights were applied, 37 countries met Criterion 1 and 24 countries met Criterion 2; when sampling weights were not applied, 56 countries met Criterion 1 and 34 countries met Criterion 2 (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">S1</ref>, <ref type="figure">Step 3</ref>).

text.text: The corresponding CFA fit statistics and measurement invariance results are reported below.

Two CFA strategies were used.
In the pooled strategy, all countries were included simultaneously and measurement invariance was evaluated across the full set of countries using multi-group CFA.

In the country-specific strategy, the four-factor CFA was first estimated separately within each country, and only countries meeting the prespecified CFA criteria were retained for subsequent multi-group invariance testing.
The reported configural, metric, scalar, and strict fit statistics for the country-specific strategy were therefore obtained from the multi-group CFA models fitted to the retained countries.

Based on the existing literature (Chen, 2007; Rutkowski & Svetina, 2014), we applied the following criteria: for metric invariance, the thresholds were |ΔCFI| < 0.02, |ΔRMSEA| < 0.03, and ΔSRMR < 0.03; for scalar or strict invariance, the thresholds were |ΔCFI| < 0.01, |ΔRMSEA| < 0.015, and ΔSRMR < 0.015.
text.formatted: Based on the existing literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Chen, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Rutkowski & Svetina, 2014)</ref>, we applied the following criteria: for metric invariance, the thresholds were |ΔCFI| < 0.02, |ΔRMSEA| < 0.03, and ΔSRMR < 0.03; for scalar or strict invariance, the thresholds were |ΔCFI| < 0.01, |ΔRMSEA| < 0.015, and ΔSRMR < 0.015.

text.text: Given that scalar and strict measurement invariance of the scale was not supported under any of the four CFA specifications, we first attempted to establish partial measurement invariance.
However, the partial invariance model did not converge and failed to yield an acceptable solution.

Therefore, to enable cross-group comparisons of the perceived scientist trustworthiness scale in a multi-country/region sample (12 items; four-factor structure: competence, integrity, benevolence, and openness), following Han's approach (Han, 2024), we further adopted measurement alignment to address cross-group non-equivalence in measurement parameters.
text.formatted: Therefore, to enable cross-group comparisons of the perceived scientist trustworthiness scale in a multi-country/region sample (12 items; four-factor structure: competence, integrity, benevolence, and openness), following Han's approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Han, 2024)</ref>, we further adopted measurement alignment to address cross-group non-equivalence in measurement parameters.

text.text: Measurement alignment was implemented based on six CFA configurational models: (1) Pooled CFA with weights (see Fig. S1, Path B1); (2) Pooled CFA without weights (see Fig. S1, Path B2); (3) Country -specific CFA with weights (see Fig. S1, Path A1) retaining countries/regions that met Criterion 1 (37 countries/regions); (4) Country -specific CFA with weights (see Fig. S1, Path A1) retaining countries/regions that met Criterion 2 (24 countries/regions); (5) Country -specific CFA with weights (see Fig. S1, Path A2) retaining countries/regions that met Criterion 1 (56 countries/regions); (6) Country -specific CFA with weights (see Fig. S1, Path A2) retaining countries/regions that met (34 countries/regions).
text.formatted: Measurement alignment was implemented based on six CFA configurational models: (1) Pooled CFA with weights (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>, Path B1); (2) Pooled CFA without weights (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>, Path B2); (3) Country -specific CFA with weights (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>, Path A1) retaining countries/regions that met Criterion 1 (37 countries/regions); (4) Country -specific CFA with weights (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>, Path A1) retaining countries/regions that met Criterion 2 (24 countries/regions); (5) Country -specific CFA with weights (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>, Path A2) retaining countries/regions that met Criterion 1 (56 countries/regions); (6) Country -specific CFA with weights (see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>, Path A2) retaining countries/regions that met (34 countries/regions).

text.text: For each configurational model, we extracted item loadings (λ) and item intercepts (ν; corresponding to the "~1" term for continuous indicators) for each country/region from the lavaan parameter estimates, and constructed "group × item" parameter matrices separately for each factor (3 items per factor).

We then conducted alignment optimization for each factor separately using the invariance. alignment function in the R package sirt, estimating aligned measurement parameters and comparable latent factor levels while allowing a subset of parameters to vary across groups.
Measurement alignment was evaluated using two complementary diagnostics: the alignment R² values for factor loadings and intercepts, and the proportion of parameters identified as noninvariant.
Following Asparouhov and Muthén (2023), the proportion of noninvariant parameters was required to remain below 20%.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Asparouhov and Muthén (2023)</ref>, the proportion of noninvariant parameters was required to remain below 20%.

text.text: For the alignment R² values, we adopted the criterion of R² > .90 proposed by Cao (2026); values below .80, particularly for intercepts, were considered indicative of poor alignment performance.
text.formatted: For the alignment R² values, we adopted the criterion of R² > .90 proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cao (2026)</ref>; values below .80, particularly for intercepts, were considered indicative of poor alignment performance.

text.text: An alignment solution was classified as acceptable only when both criteria were satisfied.
Dimensions that failed either criterion were considered unsuccessfully aligned and were excluded from subsequent analyses.
The loading and intercept tolerances used to identify noninvariant parameters, together with the corresponding R² values, are reported in Supplementary Tables S4-S9.
text.formatted: The loading and intercept tolerances used to identify noninvariant parameters, together with the corresponding R² values, are reported in Supplementary Tables <ref type="table">S4-S9</ref>.

text.text: Because the success of alignment was evaluated primarily using the alignment indices R² , we set align.pow = c(2, 2) for the loading and intercept loss functions.

This choice followed implementation-specific guidance for the sirt alignment procedure, which-drawing on comments from Alexander Robitzsch-recommends the quadratic loss function when R² is used as the principal diagnostic of alignment quality.
The default setting, align.pow = c(.25, .25), applies a more robust loss function but may produce biased R² values under some conditions.
Thus, c(2, 2) was selected to align the estimation criterion with the diagnostic used to evaluate alignment, rather than because it is uniformly preferable to the default specification.
Details of the measurement alignment procedure and results are reported below.

At the individual level, the overall score was computed as the mean of that respondent's aligned factor scores.
At the country/region level, scores were obtained by averaging individuals' overall scores within each country/region, and both weighted and unweighted country-level means were reported below.

After completing the CFA and measurement alignment procedures, we obtained a total of 12 sets of aligned scores.
These aligned scores were then entered into the regression analyses as the dependent variables (DVs), namely perceived scientist trustworthiness.

Following the approach of Cologna et al., we used multilevel linear regression to examine the associations between perceived scientist trustworthiness and perceptions of demographic, ideological, attitudinal, and country-level factors.
In the regression stage, we estimated models both with and without sampling weights.
The weights were based on WEIGHT_MLVLM, which contains rescaled poststratification weights for weighted multilevel analyses using R's lme4 package.

Rank-order stability across the three scoring approaches was evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation (1961) and Kendall's τ (1938).
text.formatted: Rank-order stability across the three scoring approaches was evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation (1961) and Kendall's τ <ref type="bibr">(1938)</ref>.

text.text: To characterize country-specific rank displacement, we calculated the absolute difference in rank positions between each pair of scoring approaches, consistent with the general logic of rank-distance measures such as Spearman's footrule (Diaconis & Graham, 1977).
text.formatted: To characterize country-specific rank displacement, we calculated the absolute difference in rank positions between each pair of scoring approaches, consistent with the general logic of rank-distance measures such as Spearman's footrule <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Diaconis & Graham, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: These differences were summarized using the median, interquartile range (IQR), and range, and the number and percentage of countries whose exact rank position changed were also reported.
The results showed that overall rank-order agreement was high, but substantial countrylevel rank changes were still observed (Table 1).
text.formatted: The results showed that overall rank-order agreement was high, but substantial countrylevel rank changes were still observed (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: The original 12-item ranking and the six-item unaligned benevolence-openness ranking showed strong agreement (Spearman's ρ = .971;
Kendall's τ = .863), as did the original and aligned rankings (Spearman's ρ = .971; Kendall's τ = .863).

Nevertheless, 62 of 68 countries (91.2%) changed their exact rank position in both comparisons, with a median absolute displacement of 3 positions (IQR = 2-5 for the original 12-item versus six-item unaligned comparison; IQR = 1.75-5 for the original versus aligned comparison; range = 0-15 for both).

Agreement between the six-item unaligned benevolenceopenness ranking and the aligned ranking was even higher (Spearman's ρ = .995; Kendall's τ = .963), yet 36 countries (52.9%) still changed rank, with a median absolute displacement of 1 position (IQR = 0-1; range = 0-11).
These findings suggest that, although the overall country rankings remained highly consistent across scoring approaches, some countries experienced changes in their relative positions.

These changes may still be substantively relevant, as even modest shifts in individual country rankings can affect the interpretation of cross-national differences, particularly when rankings are used to inform substantive conclusions or policyrelated comparisons.

To examine whether different scoring methods yielded different associations between perceived trustworthiness of scientists and the predictors, we adopted a pairwise joint multilevel linear mixed-effects modeling approach, drawing on the cross-equation coefficient comparison framework of seemingly unrelated regression (SUE; Zellner, 1962).
text.formatted: To examine whether different scoring methods yielded different associations between perceived trustworthiness of scientists and the predictors, we adopted a pairwise joint multilevel linear mixed-effects modeling approach, drawing on the cross-equation coefficient comparison framework of seemingly unrelated regression (SUE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Zellner, 1962)</ref>.

text.text: Cluster-robust variance estimation and Wald tests were used to directly assess differences in regression coefficients across scoring methods.

Three trustworthiness scores were considered: (1) the Raw4 score, calculated as the mean of available responses to 12 items covering four dimensions-competence, integrity, benevolence, and openness; (2) the Raw2 score, calculated as the mean of available responses to six items covering benevolence and openness; and (3) the Aligned score, calculated as the mean of the available measurement-aligned factor scores for benevolence and openness.

Given differences in measurement content and scoring scales, all three scores were separately standardized to Z-scores (M = 0, SD = 1) within the common analytic sample for each regression block to facilitate comparisons of regression coefficients.
Pearson correlations were also calculated to describe the linear relationships among the three scores before standardization.

Following the four sequentially adjusted regression models (Blocks 1-4) in the original analyses (Cologna et al., 2025), we conducted pairwise comparisons of the Original and Raw2 scores, the Original and Aligned scores, and the Raw2 and Aligned scores, resulting in 12 joint multilevel models.
text.formatted: Following the four sequentially adjusted regression models (Blocks 1-4) in the original analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cologna et al., 2025)</ref>, we conducted pairwise comparisons of the Original and Raw2 scores, the Original and Aligned scores, and the Raw2 and Aligned scores, resulting in 12 joint multilevel models.

text.text: The four blocks sequentially included demographic characteristics, ideological views, science-related populist attitudes and other attitudes toward science, and country-level indicators.

Within each block, all comparisons were restricted to a common analytic sample with valid observations on all three trustworthiness scores, the corresponding predictors, country identifiers, and the weighting variable.

To ensure the comparability of regression coefficients across scoring methods, a common analytic sample was used within each regression block, retaining only respondents with valid observations on all three trustworthiness scores and the corresponding predictors.
To assess the additional sample loss introduced by this restriction, we compared the sample sizes of the independently estimated models with those of the common-sample models.
The results indicated that the additional exclusions were minimal across all four blocks, with a maximum exclusion rate of only 0.042%.
In Block 4, which included all predictors, only eight additional respondents (0.019%) were excluded for both the Raw4 and Raw2 scores, while no additional exclusions occurred for the Aligned2 score.

Given the negligible additional sample loss attributable to the common-sample restriction, no additional inverse probability weighting (IPW; Cole & Hernán, 2008) adjustment was applied specifically to this restriction.
text.formatted: Given the negligible additional sample loss attributable to the common-sample restriction, no additional inverse probability weighting (IPW; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cole & Hernán, 2008)</ref> adjustment was applied specifically to this restriction.

text.text: For each pairwise comparison, the two standardized outcome scores were restructured into long format and jointly modeled, allowing separate intercepts and regression coefficients for each scoring method.

To account for the hierarchical structure of respondents nested within countries, scoring-method-specific random intercepts were specified at the country level, with separate random-intercept and residual variances across scoring methods.
The models retained the weighting variable used in the original analyses ("WEIGHT_MLVLM") and were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) (Harville, 1977; Patterson & Thompson, 1971).
text.formatted: The models retained the weighting variable used in the original analyses ("WEIGHT_MLVLM") and were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Harville, 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Patterson & Thompson, 1971)</ref>.

text.text: To account for within-country dependence and improve the robustness of statistical inference, we calculated bias-reduced cluster-robust variance estimates (CR2), with countries serving as the clustering units (Bell & Mccaffrey, 2002; Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2018).
text.formatted: To account for within-country dependence and improve the robustness of statistical inference, we calculated bias-reduced cluster-robust variance estimates (CR2), with countries serving as the clustering units <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bell & Mccaffrey, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Differences in regression coefficients across scoring methods were then evaluated using Wald tests with the Hotelling's T 2 approximation (HTZ), which provides a small-sample adjustment for hypothesis testing based on cluster-robust variance estimates (Tipton & Pustejovsky, 2015).
text.formatted: Differences in regression coefficients across scoring methods were then evaluated using Wald tests with the Hotelling's T 2 approximation (HTZ), which provides a small-sample adjustment for hypothesis testing based on cluster-robust variance estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Tipton & Pustejovsky, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, an omnibus Wald test was first conducted for each pairwise comparison to evaluate the joint null hypothesis that all corresponding predictor coefficients were equal across the two scoring methods within a given block.
Individual Wald tests were then performed to assess differences in the corresponding regression coefficients for each predictor.
For these comparisons, we reported the coefficient difference (Δβ), CR2-robust standard error (SE), 95% confidence interval (CI), and HTZ-adjusted p-value.
The coefficient difference was defined as the coefficient estimated for the first scoring method minus that estimated for the second.
Confidence intervals were calculated using CR2-robust standard errors and the approximate degrees of freedom obtained from the corresponding HTZ tests.
To control the false discovery rate associated with multiple comparisons, p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).
text.formatted: To control the false discovery rate associated with multiple comparisons, p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure <ref type="bibr">(Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: For individual coefficient comparisons, BH adjustments were applied both within each scoringmethod pair and across all three pairwise comparisons within each regression block.
For omnibus Wald tests, BH adjustments were applied across the three scoring-method comparisons within each block.

All analyses were conducted in R. Joint multilevel linear mixed-effects models were estimated using the `nlme` package (Pinheiro et al., 1999), while CR2 cluster-robust variance estimates and HTZ-adjusted Wald tests were implemented using the `clubSandwich` package (Pustejovsky, 2016).
text.formatted: All analyses were conducted in R. Joint multilevel linear mixed-effects models were estimated using the `nlme` package <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Pinheiro et al., 1999)</ref>, while CR2 cluster-robust variance estimates and HTZ-adjusted Wald tests were implemented using the `clubSandwich` package <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Pustejovsky, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Joint Wald tests revealed significant overall differences between the original fourdimensional score and the measurement-aligned two-dimensional score across all four regression blocks (all BH-adjusted ps < .001; Table S30).
text.formatted: Joint Wald tests revealed significant overall differences between the original fourdimensional score and the measurement-aligned two-dimensional score across all four regression blocks (all BH-adjusted ps < .001; Table <ref type="table">S30</ref>).

text.text: Predictor-specific comparisons indicated that these differences were concentrated in associations involving age, social dominance orientation, science-related populist attitudes, and several attitudes toward science (Table S29).
text.formatted: Predictor-specific comparisons indicated that these differences were concentrated in associations involving age, social dominance orientation, science-related populist attitudes, and several attitudes toward science (Table <ref type="table">S29</ref>).

text.text: To further distinguish the potential contributions of measurement content and alignment, we compared the original 12-item score with a six-item composite retaining only benevolence and openness.
Significant overall differences were found between these two scores across all four regression blocks (all BH-adjusted ps < .001; Table S30).
text.formatted: Significant overall differences were found between these two scores across all four regression blocks (all BH-adjusted ps < .001; Table <ref type="table">S30</ref>).

text.text: However, no significant differences were found between the original six-item composite and the measurement-aligned composite of the same two dimensions (BH-adjusted p = .096-.937; Table S30).
text.formatted: However, no significant differences were found between the original six-item composite and the measurement-aligned composite of the same two dimensions (BH-adjusted p = .096-.937; Table <ref type="table">S30</ref>).

text.text: These findings suggest that different measurement specifications of scientist trustworthiness may yield different estimates of substantive associations.

Specifically, significant differences were primarily observed between the original four-dimensional score and the two-dimensional scores, whereas no significant overall differences were found between the raw and aligned scores based on the same two dimensions.
Nevertheless, the competence and integrity dimensions did not meet the criteria for successful measurement alignment, leaving their cross-country comparability uncertain.
Therefore, rankings and substantive analyses based on the original composite score should be interpreted with caution.

These findings highlight the importance of assessing measurement invariance in cross-country/region research, as evidence of measurement comparability may inform the choice of measurement specifications and the interpretation of substantive findings.

text.text: However, the aligned scores included only two dimensions retained after alignment, whereas the original scores covered all four dimensions.
Thus, the observed differences could reflect changes in construct coverage as well as adjustments for measurement non-invariance.

Furthermore, differences in statistical significance between the original and reanalyzed regressions do not establish differences between their coefficients without a direct statistical comparison that accounts for the dependence between estimates derived from the same data.

To address these concerns, we conducted additional analyses comparing three scoring approaches: (1) the original four-factor score, (2) a six-item unaligned score from the two retained factors, and (3) the aligned two-factor score.
Respondents, countries/regions, weighting schemes, and other analytical specifications were held constant within each comparison.
